item.title: Mozilla Partners with Mistral to Bring Open-Weight AI Models to Firefox Smart Window
item.description:
Mozilla has partnered with Mistral AI to offer Mistral Small 4, an open-weight model, in Firefox's Smart Window AI assistant, now in beta. It is recommended for users in France, the US and Canada. Users can choose among several models, and Mistral agreed to zero data retention. Beta feedback is mixed.

By Daniel Curtis

item.title: What CIOs use to build an agentic enterprise
item.description:
At Bloomberg’s recent Building the Agentic Enterprise summit, in partnership with HPE, it was apparent that while most businesses and IT leaders are in the early stages of agentic AI, few have moved beyond pilots and well-fenced use cases. CIOs are clear that closing the gap is mostly an operating-model problem, not a technology one.

In a September Bloomberg Intelligence survey of 100 European and US enterprises with at least 5,000 employees, respondents put agentic multi-step workflows at just 9% when asked which use case drives the most token consumption. Coding came in at 34%, customer support at 24%, and document processing well behind that.

“We’re in the very early innings, and that quantifies how early,” Niraj Patel, senior software analyst at BI said. The barriers to scaling will sound familiar. Token and usage costs topped the list at 20%, with data privacy, regulatory compliance, unclear ROI, and integration effort close behind. Companies are attacking costs with smaller-model routing, prompt optimization, caching, fine-tuning and distillation, but Patel didn’t oversell any of them. “There’s no magic formula,” he said. “I think it’s case by case, industry by industry, company by company.”

As with internet and cloud transitions, no universal solution will benefit all companies across all industries. Instead, gen AI value will be vertically driven and sometimes company-specific as organizations rethink their operations.

Accountability doesn’t transfer to your vendor

At the summit, Daniela Dimitrova, Mercedes-Benz North America CIO, Kartik Sakthivel, CIO of John Hancock, and Rakesh Srinivasan, CDAIO and global SVP of AI, data, and emerging tech at Estée Lauder, found a lot of common ground when it comes to who controls the agent, for instance. Sakthivel reflected on how CIOs are ultimately responsible for how the agent acts. “You might have a vendor in the supply chain, and they’re responsible for their models,” he said. “But accountability ultimately rests with us.” With AI now embedded in nearly all commercial software, he said CIOs need to vet their AI vendors rigorously. “If you haven’t already, make sure you’re asking the right questions,” he added.

Sakthivel also pushed back on the AI at all cost requests that flood IT. Every agent should start with a defined business problem. Traditional software ROI models don’t fit consumption-based agentic systems, so John Hancock and its parent Manulife rebuilt their processes around consumption. He offered a test any CIO can use in that if an agent costs $200,000 to do a job a $50,000-a-year intern could handle, that’s a legitimate question to ask before anything gets built.

Pick the model for the task, not the hype

Dimitrova described a 140-year-old company using agents to reduce the complexity that has accumulated over a century. One of Mercedes-Benz USA’s first agentic use cases is in its dealer support center, which serves more than 380 dealers. Agents now handle the manual system work behind certain contract requests, turning thousands of hours a year into a few minutes, with a human in the loop deciding how far the agent goes.

On model selection, she’s practical about which models to use. “We define the model based on the task, not on hype,” she said. Mercedes stays model-agnostic and reserves expensive frontier models for complex work. A simple email draft uses a small language model.

She also addressed the presumption that governance slows innovation. Mercedes applies four principles to every agent, internal or external: responsible use with a named business owner, explainability, data protection, and safety testing before and after deployment. “Governance isn’t a roadblock,” she said. “It’s a way we can speed up implementation because we don’t have to discuss every use case.”

This gives CIOs the opportunity to redefine how people think about governance. A lot of business leaders say it gets in the way but governance that’s set once and applied everywhere becomes an accelerator. 

“We built the data foundation for the humans so they can use it with dashboards and spreadsheets,” she added. “Now we need to build it for agents as well.” That means adding a semantic layer and an ontology. Mercedes is also building a control plane for visibility across in-house, cloud, and SaaS agents, with shared components for identity, access, data, cost, and observability.

Agents have to earn trust

Srinivasan described Estée Lauder’s approach as letting agents earn autonomy over time. The company started with deterministic, data-heavy decisions such as pricing, inventory, and assortment, where speed matters and the rules are clear. Customer-facing interactions require more caution because, as he put it, a brand doesn’t get many chances to keep a customer. “If we can make anything autonomous, we would,” he said. “But the agents have to earn the trust over time.”

His MAC Cosmetics example showed why real-time data matters. Estée Lauder built an engine that captures how MAC’s makeup artists create a look and translates it into recommendations. But recommending a product that isn’t in stock damages trust. The agent is only as good as the live inventory data it relies on.

Srinivasan also offered an honest assessment of the tools market. Monitoring and managing agents at scale remain immature, and the few vendors in the space all have gaps. “You can’t buy something now that solves all the problems when it comes to monitoring agents,” he said. CIOs shouldn’t wait for a complete product. Define requirements now and assemble what you can.

But one layer often left out of agentic AI planning is the network. Every agent action moves data among applications, users, and other agents. As those agents multiply and operate at machine speed, the network becomes part of the AI system itself.

“If you’re just putting AI onto a human-speed infrastructure that’s been around for a while, all you’re doing is automating a bottleneck,” said James Robertson, global field CTO for networking at HPE.

Research shows only about 10% of companies have modernized networks with the performance and security capabilities needed to run agentic operations everywhere. Agentic traffic can place greater demands on east-west communication, alongside north-south traffic. If a breach occurs, it can spread at machine speed, so the network must have built-in observability, detection, and remediation capabilities, with automated actions operating within defined policies, permissions, and human oversight where needed. AI-driven networks with consistent zero-trust enforcement are critical to combating AI threats.

Best practices for CIOs

Pulling these threads together, top tips include:

  • Starting with the business problem and a realistic cost model. Measure the full cost of each agent action. If a person or simpler automation can do it for less, use it.
  • Rebuilding the data foundation for agents. Clean, connected, real-time data with a semantic layer is essential.
  • Making governance a platform, not a review board. Set enterprise-wide principles, assign a business owner to each agent, and use per-agent guardrails so teams can move without case-by-case debates.
  • Letting autonomy be earned. Start with low-risk, repeatable, deterministic tasks, and expand authority as performance proves itself.
  • Right-sizing your models. Match models to tasks. Frontier models for simple work are an expensive habit. In many cases, open-weight models will perform on par. Also, model innovation happens seemingly daily, so be willing to change models as needed.
  • Modernizing the network. This includes the data center network, as well as the campus, branch, and wi-fi environments. While network operations often work in silos, companies need to think of it as one network, and ensure that observability, security, and network capabilities are consistent. 
  • Investing in people as much as platforms. Sakthivel called organizational readiness one of the biggest barriers. The winners will be the companies that can reskill and upskill their people as fast as technology evolves.

item.title: Recap of Microsoft Ignite 2026: Copilot as the Work OS and Agent Governance
item.description:
At Ignite 2026, Microsoft positioned Copilot as the operating system for work and extended agent identity, governance, and cost controls across Azure, Foundry, Entra, and Defender. Highlights include Cobalt 200 VMs, Azure HorizonDB, a continuous improvement loop in Foundry, Microsoft IQ, a standalone Azure AI Gateway, and Windows Server 2028.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers
